senses.d: the horny scale of plate of epidermis at the end of the fingers and toes of man and many apes.
q: His nayles like a briddes claws were.

senses.d: The basal thickened portion of the anterior wings of certain hemiptera.
A slender, pointed piece of metal, usually with a head, used for fastening pieces of wood or other material together, by being driven into or through them.
A measure of length, being two inches and a quarter, or the sixteenth of a yard.

Nail.etym: [AS. nægel, akin to D. nagel, OS. & OHG. nagal, G. nagel, Icel. nagl, nail (in sense 1), nagli nail (in sense 3), Sw. nagel nail (in senses 1 and 3), Dan. nagle, Goth. ganagljan to nail, Lith. nagas nail (in sense 1), Russ. nogote, L. unguis, Gr. ὅνυξ, Skr. nakha. √259.]

senses.d: To fasten with a nail or nails; to close up or secure by means of nails; as, to nail boards to the beams.
q: He is now dead, and nailed in his chest.

senses.d: To stud or boss with nails, or as with nails.
q: The rivets of your arms were nailed with gold.

senses.d: To fasten, as with a nail; to bind or hold, as to a bargain or to acquiescence in an argument or assertion; hence, to catch; to trap.
q: When they came to talk of places in town, you saw at once how I nailed them.

senses.d: To spike, as a cannon.
To make naked.
q: Come, be ready, nake your swords.

senses.d: Having no clothes on; uncovered; nude; bare; as, a naked body; a naked limb; a naked sword.
Having no means of defense or protection; open; unarmed; defenseless.
q: Thy power is full naked.
Behold my bosom naked to your swords.

senses.d: Unprovided with needful or desirable accessories, means of sustenance, etc.; destitute; unaided; bare.
q: Patriots who had exposed themselves for the public, and whom they saw now left naked.

senses.d: Without addition, exaggeration, or excuses; not concealed or disguised; open to view; manifest; plain.
q: The truth appears so naked on my side, That any purblind eye may find it out.
All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.

senses.d: Mere; simple; plain.
q: The very naked name of love.

senses.d: Without pubescence; as, a naked leaf or stem; bare, or not covered by the customary parts, as a flower without a perianth, a stem without leaves, seeds without a pericarp, buds without bud scales.

Not having the full complement of tones; — said of a chord of only two tones, which requires a third tone to be sounded with them to make the combination pleasing to the ear; as, a naked fourth or fifth.

Naked.syn: Nude; bare; denuded; uncovered; unclothed; exposed; unarmed; plain; defenseless.
Naked.etym: [AS. nacod; akin to D. naakt, G. nackt, OHG. nacchot, nahhot, Icel. nökviðr, nakinn, Sw. naken, Dan. nögen, Goth. naqaþs, Lith. nůgas, Russ. nagii, L. nudus, Skr. nagna. √266. Cf. Nude.]

senses.d: The condition of being naked.
The privy parts; the genitals.
q: Ham . . . saw the nakedness of his father.

senses.d: Am not.
The title by which any person or thing is known or designated; a distinctive specific appellation, whether of an individual or a class.
q: Whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.
What's in a name? That which we call a rose By any other name would smell as sweet.

senses.d: A descriptive or qualifying appellation given to a person or thing, on account of a character or acts.
q: His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.

senses.d: Reputed character; reputation, good or bad; estimation; fame; especially, illustrious character or fame; honorable estimation; distinction.
q: What men of name resort to him?
Far above . . . every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come.
I will get me a name and honor in the kingdom.
He hath brought up an evil name upon a virgin.
The king's army . . . had left no good name behind.

senses.d: Those of a certain name; a race; a family.
q: The ministers of the republic, mortal enemies of his name, came every day to pay their feigned civilities.

senses.d: A person, an individual.
q: They list with women each degenerate name.

Name.syn: Appellation; title; designation; cognomen; denomination; epithet.
Name.etym: [AS. nama; akin to D. naam, OS. & OHG. namo, G. name, Icel. nafn, for namn, Dan. navn, Sw. namn, Goth. namō, L. nomen (perh. influenced by noscere, gnoscere, to learn to know), Gr. ὄμονα, Scr. nāman. √267. Cf. Anonymous, Ignominy, Misnomer, Nominal, Noun.]

senses.d: To give a distinctive name or appellation to; to entitle; to denominate; to style; to call.
q: She named the child Ichabod.
Thus was the building left Ridiculous, and the work Confusion named.

senses.d: To mention by name; to utter or publish the name of; to refer to by distinctive title; to mention.
q: None named thee but to praise.
Old Yew, which graspest at the stones That name the underlying dead.

senses.d: To designate by name or specifically for any purpose; to nominate; to specify; to appoint; as, to name a day for the wedding.
q: Whom late you have named for consul.

senses.d: To designate (a member) by name, as the Speaker does by way of reprimand.

Name.syn: To denominate; style; term; call; mention; specify; designate; nominate.

senses.d: By name; by particular mention; specifically; especially; expressly.
q: The solitariness of man . . . God hath namely and principally ordered to prevent by marriage.

senses.d: That is to say; to wit; videlicet; — introducing a particular or specific designation.
q: For the excellency of the soul, namely, its power of divining dreams; that several such divinations have been made, none can question.

senses.d: A little towel, or small cloth, esp. one for wiping the fingers and mouth at table.
A handkerchief.

Napkin.etym: [Dim. of OF. nape a tablecloth, cloth, F. nappe, L. mappa. See Napery.]

senses.d: A genus of endogenous bulbous plants with handsome flowers, having a cup-shaped crown within the six-lobed perianth, and comprising the daffodils and jonquils of several kinds.
A beautiful youth fabled to have been enamored of his own image as seen in a fountain, and to have been changed into the flower called Narcissus.

Narcissus.etym: [L. narcissus, and (personified) Narcissus, Gr. νάρκισσοσ, Νάρκισσοσ, fr. νάρκη torpor, in allusion to the narcotic properties of the flower. Cf. Narcotic.]

senses.d: Of little breadth; not wide or broad; having little distance from side to side; as, a narrow board; a narrow street; a narrow hem.
q: Hath passed in safety through the narrow seas.

senses.d: Of little extent; very limited; circumscribed.
q: The Jews were but a small nation, and confined to a narrow compass in the world.

senses.d: Having but a little margin; having barely sufficient space, time, or number, etc.; close; near; — with special reference to some peril or misfortune; as, a narrow shot; a narrow escape; a narrow majority.
Limited as to means; straitened; pinching; as, narrow circumstances.
Contracted; of limited scope; illiberal; bigoted; as, a narrow mind; narrow views.
Parsimonious; niggardly; covetous; selfish.
q: A very narrow and stinted charity.

senses.d: Scrutinizing in detail; close; accurate; exact.
q: But first with narrow search I must walk round This garden, and no corner leave unspied.

senses.d: Formed (as a vowel) by a close position of some part of the tongue in relation to the palate; or (according to Bell) by a tense condition of the pharynx; — distinguished from wide; as ē (ēve) and o͞o (fo͞od), etc., from ĭ (ĭll) and o͝o (fo͝ot), etc. See Guide to Pronunciation, § 13.

Narrow.etym: [OE. narwe, naru, AS. nearu; akin to OS. naru, naro.]

senses.d: A narrow passage; esp., a contracted part of a stream, lake, or sea; a strait connecting two bodies of water; — usually in the plural; as, The Narrows of New York harbor.
q: Near the island lay on one side the jaws of a dangerous narrow.

senses.d: To lessen the breadth of; to contract; to draw into a smaller compass; to reduce the width or extent of.
To contract the reach or sphere of; to make less liberal or more selfish; to limit; to confine; to restrict; as, to narrow one's views or knowledge; to narrow a question in discussion.
q: Our knowledge is much more narrowed if we confine ourselves to our own solitary reasonings.

senses.d: To contract the size of, as a stocking, by taking two stitches into one.
To become less broad; to contract; to become narrower; as, the sea narrows into a strait.
Not to step out enough to the one hand or the other; as, a horse narrows.
To contract the size of a stocking or other knit article, by taking two stitches into one.
One who, or that which, narrows or contracts.
With little breadth; in a narrow manner.
Without much extent; contractedly.
With minute scrutiny; closely; as, to look or watch narrowly; to search narrowly.
With a little margin or space; by a small distance; hence, closely; hardly; barely; only just; — often with reference to an avoided danger or misfortune; as, he narrowly escaped.
Sparingly; parsimoniously.
A part, or division, of the people of the earth, distinguished from the rest by common descent, language, or institutions; a race; a stock.
q: All nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues.

senses.d: The body of inhabitants of a country, united under an independent government of their own.
q: A nation is the unity of a people.
Praise the power that hath made and preserved us a nation.

senses.d: Family; lineage.
One of the divisions of university students in a classification according to nativity, formerly common in Europe.
A great number; a great deal; — by way of emphasis; as, a nation of herbs.

Nation.etym: [F. nation, L. natio nation, race, orig., a being born, fr. natus, p. p. of nasci, to be born, for gnatus, gnasci, from the same root as E. kin. √44. See Kin kindred, and cf. Cognate, Natal, Native.]

senses.d: Arising by birth; having an origin; born.
q: Anaximander's opinion is, that the gods are native, rising and vanishing again in long periods of times.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to one's birth; natal; belonging to the place or the circumstances in which one is born; — opposed to foreign; as, native land, language, color, etc.
Born in the region in which one lives; as, a native inhabitant, race; grown or originating in the region where used or sold; not foreign or imported; as, native oysters, or strawberries.
Original; constituting the original substance of anything; as, native dust.
Conferred by birth; derived from origin; born with one; inherent; inborn; not acquired; as, native genius, cheerfulness, simplicity, rights, etc.
q: Courage is native to you.

senses.d: Naturally related; cognate; connected (with).
q: the head is not more native to the heart, . . . Than is the throne of Denmark to thy father.

senses.d: Found in nature uncombined with other elements; as, native silver.

Native.etym: [F. natif, L. nativus, fr. nasci, p. p. natus. See Nation, and cf. Naïve, Nelf a serf.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, is born in a place or country referred to; a denizen by birth; an animal, a fruit, or vegetable, produced in a certain region; as, a native of France.
Any of the live stock found in a region, as distinguished from such as belong to pure and distinct imported breeds.
The coming into life or into the world; birth; also, the circumstances attending birth, as time, place, manner, etc.
q: I have served him from the hour of my nativity.
Thou hast left . . . the land of thy nativity.
These in their dark nativity the deep Shall yield us, pregnant with infernal flame.

senses.d: A picture representing or symbolizing the early infancy of Christ. The simplest form is the babe in a rude cradle, and the heads of an ox and an ass to express the stable in which he was born.
A representation of the positions of the heavenly bodies as the moment of one's birth, supposed to indicate his future destinies; a horoscope.

Nativity.etym: [F. nativité, L. nativitas. See Native, and cf. NaïvetÉ.]

senses.d: Fixed or determined by nature; pertaining to the constitution of a thing; belonging to native character; according to nature; essential; characteristic; not artificial, foreign, assumed, put on, or acquired; as, the natural growth of animals or plants; the natural motion of a gravitating body; natural strength or disposition; the natural heat of the body; natural color.
q: With strong natural sense, and rare force of will.

senses.d: Conformed to the order, laws, or actual facts, of nature; consonant to the methods of nature; according to the stated course of things, or in accordance with the laws which govern events, feelings, etc.; not exceptional or violent; legitimate; normal; regular; as, the natural consequence of crime; a natural death.
q: What can be more natural than the circumstances in the behavior of those women who had lost their husbands on this fatal day?

senses.d: Having to do with existing system to things; dealing with, or derived from, the creation, or the world of matter and mind, as known by man; within the scope of human reason or experience; not supernatural; as, a natural law; natural science; history, theology.
q: I call that natural religion which men might know . . . by the mere principles of reason, improved by consideration and experience, without the help of revelation.

senses.d: Conformed to truth or reality
Having the character or sentiments properly belonging to one's position; not unnatural in feelings.
q: To leave his wife, to leave his babes, . . . He wants the natural touch.

senses.d: Connected by the ties of consanguinity.
Begotten without the sanction of law; born out of wedlock; illegitimate; bastard; as, a natural child.
Of or pertaining to the lower or animal nature, as contrasted with the higher or moral powers, or that which is spiritual; being in a state of nature; unregenerate.
q: The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God.

senses.d: Belonging to, to be taken in, or referred to, some system, in which the base is 1; — said of certain functions or numbers; as, natural numbers, those commencing at 1; natural sines, cosines, etc., those taken in arcs whose radii are 1.
Produced by natural organs, as those of the human throat, in distinction from instrumental music.

Natural.etym: [OE. naturel, F. naturel, fr. L. naturalis, fr. natura. See Nature.]

senses.d: A native; an aboriginal.
Natural gifts, impulses, etc.
One born without the usual powers of reason or understanding; an idiot.
A character used to contradict, or to remove the effect of, a sharp or flat which has preceded it, and to restore the unaltered note.
In a natural manner or way; according to the usual course of things; spontaneously.
The existing system of things; the world of matter, or of matter and mind; the creation; the universe.
q: But looks through nature up to nature's God.
Nature has caprices which art can not imitate.

senses.d: The personified sum and order of causes and effects; the powers which produce existing phenomena, whether in the total or in detail; the agencies which carry on the processes of creation or of being; — often conceived of as a single and separate entity, embodying the total of all finite agencies and forces as disconnected from a creating or ordering intelligence.
q: I oft admire How Nature, wise and frugal, could commit Such disproportions.

senses.d: The established or regular course of things; usual order of events; connection of cause and effect.
Conformity to that which is natural, as distinguished from that which is artificial, or forced, or remote from actual experience.
q: One touch of nature makes the whole world kin.

senses.d: The sum of qualities and attributes which make a person or thing what it is, as distinct from others; native character; inherent or essential qualities or attributes; peculiar constitution or quality of being.
q: Thou, therefore, whom thou only canst redeem, Their nature also to thy nature join, And be thyself man among men on earth.

senses.d: Hence: Kind, sort; character; quality.
q: A dispute of this nature caused mischief.

senses.d: Physical constitution or existence; the vital powers; the natural life.
q: Oppressed nature sleeps.

senses.d: Natural affection or reverence.
q: Have we not seen The murdering son ascend his parent's bed, Through violated nature force his way?

senses.d: Constitution or quality of mind or character.
q: A born devil, on whose nature Nurture can never stick.
That reverence which is due to a superior nature.

Nature.etym: [F., fr. L. natura, fr. natus born, produced, p. p. of nasci to be born. See Nation.]

senses.d: To endow with natural qualities.
q: He which natureth every kind.

senses.d: Nothing.
q: Doth Job fear God for naught?

senses.d: The arithmetical character 0; a cipher. See Cipher.

Naught.etym: [OE. naught, nought, naht, nawiht, AS. nāwiht, nāuht, nāht; ne not + ā ever + wiht thing, whit; hence, not ever a whit. See No, adv. Whit, and cf. Aught, Not.]

senses.d: In no degree; not at all.
q: To wealth or sovereign power he naught applied.

senses.d: Of no value or account; worthless; bad; useless.
q: It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer.
Go, get you to your house; begone, away! All will be naught else.
Things naught and things indifferent.

senses.d: Hence, vile; base; naughty.
q: No man can be stark naught at once.

senses.d: The quality or state of being naughty; perverseness; badness; wickedness.
q: I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart.

senses.d: Having little or nothing.
q: that needy be and naughty, help them with thy goods.

senses.d: Worthless; bad; good for nothing.
q: The other basket had very naughty figs.

senses.d: hence, corrupt; wicked.
q: So shines a good deed in a naughty world.

senses.d: Mischievous; perverse; froward; guilty of disobedient or improper conduct; as, a naughty child.
The block in the center of a wheel, from which the spokes radiate, and through which the axle passes; — called also hub or hob.
The navel.

Nave.etym: [AS. nafu; akin to D. naaf, G. nabe, OHG. naba, Icel. nöf, Dan. nav, Sw. naf, Skr. nābhi nave and navel: cf. L. umbo boss of a shield. √260. Cf. Navel.]

senses.d: The middle or body of a church, extending from the transepts to the principal entrances, or, if there are no transepts, from the choir to the principal entrance, but not including the aisles.

Nave.etym: [F. nef, fr. L. navis ship, to which the church was often likened; akin to Gr. ναύαρχόσ, Skr. nāus, and perh. to AS. naca boat, G. nachen, Icel. nökkvi; cf. L. nare to swim, float. Cf. Nausea, Nautical, Naval.]

senses.d: A mark or depression in the middle of the abdomen; the umbilicus. See Umbilicus.
The central part or point of anything; the middle.
q: Within the navel of this hideous wood, Immured in cypress shades, a sorcerer dwells.

senses.d: An eye on the under side of a carronade for securing it to a carriage.

Navel.etym: [AS. nafela, fr. nafu nave; akin to D. navel, G. nabel, OHG. nabolo, Icel. nafli, Dan. navle, Sw. nafle, L. umbilicus, Gr. ομφαλὄσ, Skr. nābhīla. √260. See Nave hub, and cf. Omphalic, Nombril, Umbilical.]

senses.d: A fleet of ships; an assemblage of merchantmen, or so many as sail in company.
The whole of the war vessels belonging to a nation or ruler, considered collectively; as, the navy of Italy.
The officers and men attached to the war vessels of a nation; as, he belongs to the navy.

Navy.etym: [ OF. navie, fr. L. navis ship. See Nave of a church.]

senses.d: No; — a negative answer to a question asked, or a request made, now superseded by no. See Yes.
q: And eke when I say “ye,” ne say not “nay.”
I tell you nay; but except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
And now do they thrust us out privily? nay, verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out.
He that will not when he may, When he would he shall have nay.

senses.d: Not this merely, but also; not only so, but; — used to mark the addition or substitution of a more explicit or more emphatic phrase.

Nay.etym: [Icel. nei; akin to E. no. See No, adv.]

senses.d: Denial; refusal.
A negative vote; one who votes in the negative.
To refuse.
A native or inhabitant of Nazareth; — a term of contempt applied to Christ and the early Christians.
One of a sect of Judaizing Christians in the first and second centuries, who observed the laws of Moses, and held to certain heresies.

A Jew bound by a vow to leave the hair uncut, to abstain from wine and strong drink, and to practice extraordinary purity of life and devotion, the obligation being for life, or for a certain time. The word is also used adjectively.
Not; never.
q: He never yet no villany ne said.

senses.d: Nor.
q: No niggard ne no fool.

senses.d: At a little distance, in place, time, manner, or degree; not remote; nigh.
q: My wife! my traitress! let her not come near me.

senses.d: Nearly; almost; well-nigh.
q: Near about the yearly value of the land.

senses.d: Closely; intimately.

Near.etym: [AS. neár, compar. of neáh nigh. See Nigh.]

senses.d: Not far distant in time, place, or degree; not remote; close at hand; adjacent; neighboring; nigh.
q: He served great Hector, and was ever near, Not with his trumpet only, but his spear.

senses.d: Closely connected or related.
q: She is thy father's near kinswoman.

senses.d: Close to one's interests, affection, etc.; touching, or affecting intimately; intimate; dear; as, a near friend.
Close to anything followed or imitated; not free, loose, or rambling; as, a version near to the original.
So as barely to avoid or pass injury or loss; close; narrow; as, a near escape.
Next to the driver, when he is on foot; in the Unted States, on the left of an animal or a team; as, the near ox; the near leg. See Off side, under Off, a.
Immediate; direct; close; short.
Close-fisted; parsimonious.

Near.syn: Nigh; close; adjacent; proximate; contiguous; present; ready; intimate; familiar; dear.

senses.d: Adjacent to; close by; not far from; nigh; as, the ship sailed near the land. See the Note under near, a.
To approach; to come nearer; as, the ship neared the land.
To draw near; to approach.
q: A speck, a mist, a shape, I wist! And still it neared, and neared.

senses.d: Such as must be; impossible to be otherwise; not to be avoided; inevitable.
q: Death, a necessary end, Will come when it will come.

senses.d: Impossible to be otherwise, or to be dispensed with, without preventing the attainment of a desired result; indispensable; requisite; essential.
q: A certain kind of temper is necessary to the pleasure and quiet of our minds.

senses.d: Acting from necessity or compulsion; involuntary; — opposed to free; as, whether man is a necessary or a free agent is a question much discussed.

Necessary.etym: [L. necessarius, from necesse unavoidable, necessary; of uncertain origin: cf. F. nécessaire.]

senses.d: A thing that is necessary or indispensable to some purpose; something that one can not do without; a requisite; an essential; — used chiefly in the plural; as, the necessaries of life.
A privy; a water-closet.
Such things, in respect to infants, lunatics, and married women, as are requisite for support suitable to station.
The quality or state of being necessary, unavoidable, or absolutely requisite; inevitableness; indispensableness.
The condition of being needy or necessitous; pressing need; indigence; want.
q: Urge the necessity and state of times.
The extreme poverty and necessity his majesty was in.

senses.d: That which is necessary; a necessary; a requisite; something indispensable; — often in the plural.
q: These should be hours for necessities, Not for delights.
What was once to me Mere matter of the fancy, now has grown The vast necessity of heart and life.

senses.d: That which makes an act or an event unavoidable; irresistible force; overruling power; compulsion, physical or moral; fate; fatality.
q: So spake the fiend, and with necessity, The tyrant's plea, excused his devilish deeds.

senses.d: The negation of freedom in voluntary action; the subjection of all phenomena, whether material or spiritual, to inevitable causation; necessitarianism.

Necessity.etym: [OE. necessite, F. nécessité, L. necessitas, fr. necesse. See Necessary.]

senses.d: The part of an animal which connects the head and the trunk, and which, in man and many other animals, is more slender than the trunk.
Any part of an inanimate object corresponding to or resembling the neck of an animal
A reduction in size near the end of an object, formed by a groove around it; as, a neck forming the journal of a shaft.
the point where the base of the stem of a plant arises from the root.

Neck.etym: [OE. necke, AS. hnecca; akin to D. nek the nape of the neck, G. nacken, OHG. nacch, hnacch, Icel. hnakki, Sw. nacke, Dan. nakke.]

senses.d: To reduce the diameter of (an object) near its end, by making a groove around it; — used with down; as, to neck down a shaft.
One who practices necromancy; a sorcerer; a wizard.
Born; — a term sometimes used in introducing the name of the family to which a married woman belongs by birth; as, Madame de Staël, née Necker.

Nee.etym: [F., fr. L. nata, fem. of natus, p. p. of nasci to be born. See Nation.]

senses.d: A state that requires supply or relief; pressing occasion for something; necessity; urgent want.
q: And the city had no need of the sun.
I have no need to beg.
Be governed by your needs, not by your fancy.

senses.d: Want of the means of subsistence; poverty; indigence; destitution.
q: Famine is in thy cheeks; Need and oppression starveth in thine eyes.

senses.d: That which is needful; anything necessary to be done; (pl.) necessary things; business.
Situation of need; peril; danger.

Need.syn: Exigency; emergency; strait; extremity; necessity; distress; destitution; poverty; indigence; want; penury.
Need.etym: [OE. need, neod, nede, AS. neád, nȳd; akin to D. nood, G. not, noth, Icel. nauðr, Sw. & Dan. nöd, Goth. nauþs.]

senses.d: To be in want of; to have cause or occasion for; to lack; to require, as supply or relief.
q: Other creatures all day long Rove idle, unemployed, and less need rest.

Need.etym: [See Need, n. Cf. AS. nȳdan to force, Goth. nauþjan.]

senses.d: To be wanted; to be necessary.
q: When we have done it, we have done all that is in our power, and all that needs.

senses.d: Of necessity. See Needs.
Full of need; in need or want; needy; distressing.
q: The needful time of trouble.

senses.d: Necessary for supply or relief; requisite.
q: All things needful for defense abound.

senses.d: A small instrument of steel, sharply pointed at one end, with an eye to receive a thread, — used in sewing.

A slender rod or wire used in knitting; a knitting needle; also, a hooked instrument which carries the thread or twine, and by means of which knots or loops are formed in the process of netting, knitting, or crocheting.
One of the needle-shaped secondary leaves of pine trees. See Pinus.
Any slender, pointed object, like a needle, as a pointed crystal, a sharp pinnacle of rock, an obelisk, etc.

Needle.etym: [OE. nedle, AS. nǣdl; akin to D. neald, OS. nādla, G. nadel, OHG. nādal, nādala, Icel. nāl, Sw. nål, Dan. naal, and also to G. nähen to sew, OHG. nājan, L. nere to spin, Gr. νέειν, and perh. to E. snare: cf. Gael. & Ir. snathad needle, Gael. snath thread, G. schnur string, cord.]

senses.d: To form in the shape of a needle; as, to needle crystals.
To form needles; to crystallize in the form of needles.
Work executed with a needle; sewed work; sewing; embroidery; also, the business of a seamstress.
The combination of timber and plaster making the outside framework of some houses.
Of necessity; necessarily; indispensably; — often with must, and equivalent to of need.
q: A man must needs love mauger his head.
And he must needs go through Samaria.
He would needs know the cause of his repulse.

Needs.etym: [Orig. gen. of need, used as an adverb. Cf. -wards.]

senses.d: Distressed by want of the means of living; very poor; indigent; necessitous.
q: Thou shalt open thy hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy in thy land.
Spare the blushes of needy merit.

senses.d: Necessary; requisite.
q: Corn to make your needy bread.

senses.d: Sneezing.

Not to attend to with due care or attention; to forbear one's duty in regard to; to suffer to pass unimproved, unheeded, undone, etc.; to omit; to disregard; to slight; as, to neglect duty or business; to neglect to pay debts.
q: I hope My absence doth neglect no great designs.
This, my long suffering and my day of grace, Those who neglect and scorn shall never taste.

senses.d: To omit to notice; to forbear to treat with attention or respect; to slight; as, to neglect strangers.

Neglect.syn: To slight; overlook; disregard; disesteem; contemn. See Slight.
Neglect.etym: [L. neglectus, p. p. of neglegere (negligere) to disregard, neglect, the literal sense prob. being, not to pick up; nec not, nor (fr. ne not + -que, a particle akin to Goth. -h, -uh, and prob. to E. who; cf. Goth. nih nor) + L. legere to pick up, gather. See No, adv., Legend, Who.]

senses.d: Omission of proper attention; avoidance or disregard of duty, from heedlessness, indifference, or willfulness; failure to do, use, or heed anything; culpable disregard; as, neglect of business, of health, of economy.
q: To tell thee sadly, shepherd, without blame, Or our neglect, we lost her as we came.

senses.d: Omission of attention or civilities; slight; as, neglect of strangers.
Habitual carelessness; negligence.
q: Age breeds neglect in all.

senses.d: The state of being disregarded, slighted, or neglected.
q: Rescue my poor remains from vile neglect.

Neglect.syn: Negligence; inattention; disregard; disesteem; remissness; indifference. See Negligence.

senses.d: Apt to neglect; customarily neglectful; characterized by negligence; careless; heedless; culpably careless; showing lack of attention; as, disposed in negligent order.
q: He that thinks he can afford to be negligent is not far from being poor.

Negligent.syn: Careles; heedless; neglectful; regardless; thoughtless; indifferent; inattentive; remiss.
Negligent.etym: [F. négligent, L. negligens,p. pr. of negligere. See Neglect.]

senses.d: A thing of brass; — the name under which the Israelites worshiped the brazen serpent made by Moses.
To utter the cry of the horse; to whinny.
To scoff or sneer; to jeer.
q: Neighed at his nakedness.

Neigh.etym: [OE. neien, AS. hnǣgan, prob. of imitative origin; cf. MHG. nēgen, Icel. hneggja, gneggja, Sw. gnägga. Cf. Nag a horse.]

senses.d: The cry of a horse; a whinny.
Not either; not the one or the other.
q: Which of them shall I take? Both? one? or neither? Neither can be enjoyed, If both remain alive.
He neither loves, Nor either cares for him.

Neither.etym: [OE. neither, nother, nouther, AS. nāwðer, nāhwæðer; nā never, not + hwæðer whether. The word has followed the form of either. See No, and Whether, and cf. Neuter, Nor.]

senses.d: Not either; generally used to introduce the first of two or more coördinate clauses of which those that follow begin with nor.
q: Fight neither with small nor great, save only with the king.
Hadst thou been firm and fixed in thy dissent, Neither had I transgressed, nor thou with me.
When she put it on, she made me vow That I should neither sell, nor give, nor lose it.

senses.d: A grandson or grandchild, or remoter lineal descendant.
q: But if any widow have children or nephews [Rev. Ver. grandchildren].
If naturalists say true that nephews are often liker to their grandfathers than to their fathers.

senses.d: A cousin.
The son of a brother or a sister, or of a brother-in-law or sister-in-law.

Nephew.etym: [OE. neveu, nevou, nevu, fr. F. neveu, OF. also, nevou, L. nepos; akin to AS. nefa, D. neef, G. neffe, OHG. nevo, Icel. nefi a kinsman, Gr. νέποδεσ, pl., brood, young, Skr. nepāt grandson, descendant. √262. Cf. Niece, Nepotism.]

senses.d: Nearer.
The bed or receptacle prepared by a fowl for holding her eggs and for hatching and rearing her young.
q: The birds of the air have nests.

senses.d: Hence: the place in which the eggs of other animals, as insects, turtles, etc., are laid and hatched; a snug place in which young animals are reared.

A snug, comfortable, or cozy residence or situation; a retreat, or place of habitual resort; hence, those who occupy a nest, frequent a haunt, or are associated in the same pursuit; as, a nest of traitors; a nest of bugs.
q: A little cottage, like some poor man's nest.

senses.d: An aggregated mass of any ore or mineral, in an isolated state, within a rock.
A collection of boxes, cases, or the like, of graduated size, each put within the one next larger.
A compact group of pulleys, gears, springs, etc., working together or collectively.

Nest.etym: [AS. nest; akin to D. & G. nest, Sw. näste, L. nidus, for nisdus, Skr. nīḍa resting place, nest; cf. Lith. lizdas, Arm. neiz, Gael. & Ir. nead. Prob. from the particle ni down, Skr. ni + the root of E. sit, and thus orig., a place to sit down in. √ 264. See Nether, and Sit, and cf. Eyas, Nidificatio

senses.d: To build and occupy a nest.
q: The king of birds nested within his leaves.

senses.d: To put into a nest; to form a nest for.
q: From him who nested himself into the chief power.

senses.d: A fabric of twine, thread, or the like, wrought or woven into meshes, and used for catching fish, birds, butterflies, etc.
Anything designed or fitted to entrap or catch; a snare; any device for catching and holding.
q: A man that flattereth his neighbor spreadeth a net for his feet.
In the church's net there are fishes good or bad.

senses.d: Anything wrought or woven in meshes; as, a net for the hair; a mosquito net; a tennis net.
A figure made up of a large number of straight lines or curves, which are connected at certain points and related to each other by some specified law.

Net.etym: [AS. net; akin to D. net, OS. net, netti, OHG. nezzi, G. netz, Icel. & Dan. net, Sw. nät, Goth. nati; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To make into a net; to make in the style of network; as, to net silk.
To take in a net; to capture by stratagem or wile.
q: And now I am here, netted and in the toils.

senses.d: To inclose or cover with a net; as, to net a tree.
To form network or netting; to knit.
Without spot; pure; shining.
q: Her breast all naked as net ivory.

senses.d: Free from extraneous substances; pure; unadulterated; neat; as, net wine, etc.
Not including superfluous, incidental, or foreign matter, as boxes, coverings, wraps, etc.; free from charges, deductions, etc; as, net profit; net income; net weight, etc.
To produce or gain as clear profit; as, he netted a thousand dollars by the operation.
Situated down or below; lying beneath, or in the lower part; having a lower position; belonging to the region below; lower; under; — opposed to upper.
q: 'Twixt upper, nether, and surrounding fires.
This darksome nether world her light Doth dim with horror and deformity.
All my nether shape thus grew transformed.

Nether.etym: [OE. nethere, neithere, AS. niðera, fr. the adv. niðer downward; akin to neoðan below, beneath, D. neder down, G. nieder, Sw. nedre below, nether, a. & adv., and also to Skr. ni down. √201. Cf. Beneath.]

senses.d: Lowest; as, the nethermost abyss.

Nethermost.etym: [AS. niðemest. See Nether, and cf. Aftermost.]

senses.d: Servants of the priests and Levites in the menial services about the tabernacle and temple.

Nethinim.etym: [Heb., pl. of nāthīn given, granted, a slave of the temple, fr. nāthan to give.]

senses.d: A plant of the genus Urtica, covered with minute sharp hairs containing a poison that produces a stinging sensation. Urtica gracilis is common in the Northern, and U. chamædryoides in the Southern, United States. The common European species, U. urens and U. dioica, are also found in the Eastern united States. U. pilulifera is the Roman nettle of England.

Nettle.etym: [AS. netele; akin to D. netel, G. nessel, OHG. nezzïla, nazza, Dan. nelde, nälde, Sw. nässla; cf, Lith. notere.]

senses.d: To fret or sting; to irritate or vex; to cause to experience sensations of displeasure or uneasiness not amounting to violent anger.
q: The princes were so nettled at the scandal of this affront, that every man took it to himself.

senses.d: The halves of yarns in the unlaid end of a rope twisted for pointing or grafting.
Small lines used to sling hammocks under the deck beams.
Reef points.
A fabric of threads, cords, or wires crossing each other at certain intervals, and knotted or secured at the crossings, thus leaving spaces or meshes between them.
Any system of lines or channels interlacing or crossing like the fabric of a net; as, a network of veins; a network of railroads.
Not ever; not at any time; at no time, whether past, present, or future.
q: Death still draws nearer, never seeming near.

senses.d: In no degree; not in the least; not.
q: Whosoever has a friend to guide him, may carry his eyes in another man's head, and yet see never the worse.
And he answered him to never a word.

Never.etym: [AS. nǣfre; ne not, no + ǣfre ever.]

senses.d: Not the less; notwithstanding; in spite of that; yet.
q: No chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous; nevertheless, afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness.

Nevertheless.syn: However; at least; yet; still. See However.

senses.d: Having existed, or having been made, but a short time; having originated or occured lately; having recently come into existence, or into one's possession; not early or long in being; of late origin; recent; fresh; modern; — opposed to old, as, a new coat; a new house; a new book; a new fashion.
Not before seen or known, although existing before; lately manifested; recently discovered; as, a new metal; a new planet; new scenes.
Newly beginning or recurring; starting anew; now commencing; different from what has been; as, a new year; a new course or direction.
As if lately begun or made; having the state or quality of original freshness; also, changed for the better; renovated; unworn; untried; unspent; as, rest and travel made him a new man.
q: Steadfasty purposing to lead a new life.
Men after long emaciating diets, fat, and almost new.

senses.d: Not of ancient extraction, or of a family of ancient descent; not previously known or famous.
Not habituated; not familiar; unaccustomed.
q: New to the plow, unpracticed in the trace.

senses.d: Fresh from anything; newly come.
q: New from her sickness to that northern air.

New.syn: Novel; recent; fresh; modern. See Novel.
New.etym: [OE. OE. newe, AS. niwe, neowe; akin to D. nieuw, OS. niwi, OHG. niuwi, G. neu, Icel. nȳr, Dan. & Sw. ny, Goth. niujis, Lith. naujas, Russ. novuii, Ir. nua, nuadh, Gael. nuadh, W. newydd, Armor. nevez, L. novus, Gr. νέοσ, Skr. nava, and prob. to E. now. √263. See Now, and cf. Announce, Innovate, Neo

senses.d: Newly; recently.
To make new; to renew.
Recently born.
Lately; recently.
q: He rubbed it o'er with newly gathered mint.

senses.d: Anew; afresh; freshly.
q: And the refined mind doth newly fashion Into a fairer form.

senses.d: The quality or state of being new; as, the newness of a system; the newness of a scene; newness of life.
A report of recent occurrences; information of something that has lately taken place, or of something before unknown; fresh tidings; recent intelligence.
q: Evil news rides post, while good news baits.

senses.d: Something strange or newly happened.
q: It is no news for the weak and poor to be a prey to the strong and rich.

senses.d: A bearer of news; a courier; a newspaper.
q: There cometh a news thither with his horse.

News.etym: [From New; cf. F. nounelles. News is plural in form, but is commonly used with a singular verb.]

senses.d: Nearest in place; having no similar object intervening.
q: Her princely guest Was next her side; in order sat the rest.
Fear followed me so hard, that I fled the next way.

senses.d: Nearest in time; as, the next day or hour.
Adjoining in a series; immediately preceding or following in order.
q: None could tell whose turn should be the next.

senses.d: Nearest in degree, quality, rank, right, or relation; as, the next heir was an infant.
q: The man is near of kin unto us, one of our next kinsmen.

Next.etym: [AS. nēhst, niéhst, nȳhst, superl. of neáh nigh. See Nigh.]

senses.d: In the time, place, or order nearest or immediately succeeding; as, this man follows next.
One of certain corrupt persons in the early church at Ephesus, who are censured in Rev. ii. 6, 15.

Nicolaitan.etym: [So called from Nicolas of Antioch, mentioned in Acts vi. 5.]

senses.d: Not distant or remote in place or time; near.
q: The loud tumult shows the battle nigh.

senses.d: Not remote in degree, kindred, circumstances, etc.; closely allied; intimate.
q: Ye . . . are made nigh by the blood of Christ.

Nigh.syn: Near; close; adjacent; contiguous; present; neighboring.
Nigh.etym: [OE. nigh, neigh, neih, AS. neáh, nēh; akin to D. na, adv., OS. nāh, a., OHG. nāh, G. nah, a., nach to, after, Icel. nā (in comp.) nigh, Goth. nēhw, nēhwa, adv., nigh. Cf. Near, Neighbor, Next.]

senses.d: In a situation near in place or time, or in the course of events; near.
q: He was sick, nigh unto death.
He drew not nigh unheard; the angel bright, Ere he drew nigh, his radiant visage turned.

senses.d: Almost; nearly; as, he was nigh dead.
To draw nigh (to); to approach; to come near.
Near to; not remote or distant from.

That part of the natural day when the sun is beneath the horizon, or the time from sunset to sunrise; esp., the time between dusk and dawn, when there is no light of the sun, but only moonlight, starlight, or artificial light.
q: And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.

senses.d: Darkness; obscurity; concealment.
q: Nature and nature's laws lay hid in night.

senses.d: Intellectual and moral darkness; ignorance.
A state of affliction; adversity; as, a dreary night of sorrow.
The period after the close of life; death.
q: She closed her eyes in everlasting night.

senses.d: A lifeless or unenlivened period, as when nature seems to sleep.

Night.etym: [OE. night, niht, AS. neaht, niht; akin to D. nacht, OS. & OHG. naht, G. nacht, Icel. n�tt, Sw. natt, Dan. nat, Goth. nachts, Lith. naktis, Russ. noche, W. nos, Ir. nochd, L. nox, noctis, Gr. �, �, Skr. nakta, nakti. √ 265. Cf. Equinox, Nocturnal.]

senses.d: Not in.
Eight and one more; one less than ten; as, nine miles.

Nine.etym: [OE. nine, nihen, AS. nigon, nigan; akin to D. & LG. negen, OS. & OFries. nigun, OHG. niun, G. neun, Icel. nīu, sw. nio, Dan. ni, Goth. niun, Ir. & Gael. naoi, W. naw, L. novem, Gr. εννἔα, Skr. navan; of unknown origin. √307. Cf. Novembeer.]

senses.d: The number greater than eight by a unit; nine units or objects.
A symbol representing nine units, as 9 or ix.
Nine and ten; eighteen and one more; one less than twenty; as, nineteen months.

Nineteen.etym: [AS. nigontȳne, nigontēne. See Nine, and Ten.]

senses.d: The number greater than eighteen by a unit; the sum of ten and nine; nineteen units or objects.
A symbol for nineteen units, as 19 or xix.
Following the eighteenth and preceding the twentieth; coming after eighteen others.
Constituting or being one of nineteen equal parts into which anything is divided.
The quotient of a unit divided by nineteen; one of nineteen equal parts of anything.
The next in order after the eighteenth.
An interval of two octaves and a fifth.
Nine times ten; eighty-nine and one more; as, ninety men.
The sum of nine times ten; the number greater by a unit than eighty-nine; ninety units or objects.
A symbol representing ninety units, as 90 or xc.
Following the eight and preceding the tenth; coming after eight others.
Constituting or being one of nine equal parts into which anything is divided.
The quotient of one divided by nine; one of nine equal parts of a thing; the next after the eighth.
An interval containing an octave and a second.
The first month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, formerly answering nearly to the month of April, now to March, of the Christian calendar. See Abib.
Not any; not one; none.
q: Let there be no strife . . . between me and thee.
That goodness is no name, and happiness no dream.

No.etym: [OE. no, non, the same word as E. none; cf. E. a, an. See None.]

senses.d: Nay; not; not at all; not in any respect or degree; — a word expressing negation, denial, or refusal. Before or after another negative, no is emphatic.
q: We do no otherwise than we are willed.
I am perplx'd and doubtful whether or no I dare accept this your congratulation.
There is none righteous, no, not one.
No! Nay, Heaven forbid.

No.etym: [OE. no, na, AS. nā; ne not + ā ever. AS. ne is akin to OHG. ni, Goth. ni, Russ. ne, Ir., Gael. & W. ni, L. ne, Gr. νη (in comp.), Skr. na, and also to E. prefix un-. √ 193. See Aye, and cf. Nay, Not, Nice, Nefarious.]

senses.d: A refusal by use of the wordd no; a denial.
A negative vote; one who votes in the negative; as, to call for the ayes and noes; the noes have it.
A patriarch of Biblical history, in the time of the Deluge.
The head.
A person in a superior position in life; a nobleman.
Possessing eminence, elevation, dignity, etc.; above whatever is low, mean, degrading, or dishonorable; magnanimous; as, a noble nature or action; a noble heart.
q: Statues, with winding ivy crowned, belong To nobler poets for a nobler song.

senses.d: Grand; stately; magnificent; splendid; as, a noble edifice.
Of exalted rank; of or pertaining to the nobility; distinguished from the masses by birth, station, or title; highborn; as, noble blood; a noble personage.

Noble.syn: Honorable; worthy; dignified; elevated; exalted; superior; sublime; great; eminent; illustrious; renowned; stately; splendid; magnificent; grand; magnanimous; generous; liberal; free.
Noble.etym: [F. noble, fr. L. nobilis that can be or is known, well known, famous, highborn, noble, fr. noscere to know. See know.]

senses.d: A person of rank above a commoner; a nobleman; a peer.
An English money of account, and, formerly, a gold coin, of the value of 6 s. 8 d. sterling, or about $1.61.
A European fish; the lyrie.
To make noble; to ennoble.
q: Thou nobledest so far forth our nature.

senses.d: One of the nobility; a noble; a peer; one who enjoys rank above a commoner, either by virtue of birth, by office, or by patent.
To bend or incline the upper part, with a quick motion; as, nodding plumes.
To incline the head with a quick motion; to make a slight bow; to make a motion of assent, of salutation, or of drowsiness, with the head; as, to nod at one.
To be drowsy or dull; to be careless.
q: Nor is it Homer nods, but we that dream.

Nod.etym: [OE. nodden; cf. OHG. knōtōn, genuotōn, to shake, and E. nudge.]

senses.d: To incline or bend, as the head or top; to make a motion of assent, of salutation, or of drowsiness with; as, to nod the head.
To signify by a nod; as, to nod approbation.
To cause to bend.
q: By every wind that nods the mountain pine.

senses.d: A dropping or bending forward of the upper part or top of anything.
q: Like a drunken sailor on a mast, Ready with every nod to tumble down.

senses.d: A quick or slight downward or forward motion of the head, in assent, in familiar salutation, in drowsiness, or in giving a signal, or a command.
q: A look or a nod only ought to correct them when they do amiss.
Nations obey my word and wait my nod.

senses.d: Sound of any kind.
q: The heavens turn about in a most rapid motion without noise to us perceived.

senses.d: Especially, loud, confused, or senseless sound; clamor; din.
Loud or continuous talk; general talk or discussion; rumor; report.
q: What noise have we had about transplantation of diseases and transfusion of blood!
Socrates lived in Athens during the great plague which has made so much noise in all ages.

senses.d: Music, in general; a concert; also, a company of musicians; a band.
q: The king has his noise of gypsies.

Noise.syn: Cry; outcry; clamor; din; clatter; uproar.
Noise.etym: [F. noise noisy strife, quarrel, brawl, fr. L. nausea seasickness, sickness, disgust. See Nausea.]

senses.d: To sound; to make a noise.
To spread by rumor or report.
q: All these sayings were noised abroad.

senses.d: To disturb with noise.
Noxious to health; hurtful; mischievous; unwholesome; insalubrious; destructive; as, noisome effluvia.
Offensive to the smell or other senses; disgusting; fetid.

Noisome.etym: [For noysome, fr. noy for annoy. See Annoy.]

senses.d: No; not. See No, a.
No one; not one; not anything; — frequently used also partitively, or as a plural, not any.
q: There is none that doeth good; no, not one.
Six days ye shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is the Sabbath, in it there shall be none.
Terms of peace yet none Vouchsafed or sought.
None of their productions are extant.

senses.d: No; not any; — used adjectively before a vowel, in old style; as, thou shalt have none assurance of thy life.

None.etym: [OE. none, non, nan, no, na, AS. nān, fr. ne not + ān one. √193. See No, a. & adv., One, and cf. Non-, Null, a.]

senses.d: Same as Nones, 2.
No. See the Note under No.
The middle of the day; midday; the time when the sun is in the meridian; twelve o'clock in the daytime.
Hence, the highest point; culmination.
q: In the very noon of that brilliant life which was destined to be so soon, and so fatally, overshadowed.

Noon.etym: [AS. nōn, orig., the ninth hour, fr. L. nona (sc. hora) the ninth hour, then applied to the church services (called nones) at that hour, the time of which was afterwards changed to noon. See Nine, and cf. Nones, Nunchion.]

senses.d: Belonging to midday; occurring at midday; meridional.
To take rest and refreshment at noon.
Midday; twelve o'clock in the day; noon.
Of or pertaining to midday; meridional; as, the noonday heat.
The time of noon; midday.

Noontide.etym: [From noon + tide time; cf. AS. nōntīd the ninth hour.]

senses.d: A negative connective or particle, introducing the second member or clause of a negative proposition, following neither, or not, in the first member or clause (as or in affirmative propositions follows either). Nor is also used sometimes in the first member for neither, and sometimes the neither is omitted and implied by the use of nor.
q: Provide neither gold nor silver, nor brass, in your purses, nor scrip for your journey.
Where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt.
I love him not, nor fear him.
Where neither party is nor true, nor kind.
Simois nor Xanthus shall be wanting there.

Nor.etym: [OE. nor, contr. from nother. See Neither.]

senses.d: That one of the four cardinal points of the compass, at any place, which lies in the direction of the true meridian, and to the left hand of a person facing the east; the direction opposite to the south.
Any country or region situated farther to the north than another; the northern section of a country.
Specifically: That part of the United States lying north of Mason and Dixon's line. See under Line.

North.etym: [AS. norð; akin to D. noord, G., Sw., & Dan. nord, Icel. norðr. Cf. Norman, Norse.]

senses.d: Lying toward the north; situated at the north, or in a northern direction from the point of observation or reckoning; proceeding toward the north, or coming from the north.
To turn or move toward the north; to veer from the east or west toward the north.
Northward.
Of or pertaining to the north; being in the north, or nearer to that point than to the east or west.
In a direction toward the north; as, to steer a northern course; coming from the north; as, a northern wind.
Toward the north; nearer to the north than to the east or west point.
Toward the north, or toward a point nearer to the north than to the east or west point.
The prominent part of the face or anterior extremity of the head containing the nostrils and olfactory cavities; the olfactory organ. See Nostril, and Olfactory organ under Olfactory.
The power of smelling; hence, scent.
q: We are not offended with a dog for a better nose than his master.

senses.d: A projecting end or beak at the front of an object; a snout; a nozzle; a spout; as, the nose of a bellows; the nose of a teakettle.

Nose.etym: [AS. nosu; akin to D. neus, G. nase, OHG. nasa, Icel. nös, Sw. näsa, Dan. näse, Lith. nosis, Russ. nos', L. nasus, nares, Skr. nāsā, nās. √261. Cf. Nasal, Nasturtium, Naze, Nostril, Nozzle.]

senses.d: To smell; to scent; hence, to track, or trace out.
To touch with the nose; to push the nose into or against; hence, to interfere with; to treat insolently.
q: Lambs . . . nosing the mother's udder.
A sort of national convention, dubious in its nature . . . nosed Parliament in the very seat of its authority.

senses.d: To utter in a nasal manner; to pronounce with a nasal twang; as, to nose a prayer.
To smell; to sniff; to scent.
To pry officiously into what does not concern one.
To confront; be closely face to face or opposite to; meet.
To furnish with a nose; as, to nose a stair tread.
To examine with the nose or sense of smell.
To make by advancing the nose or front end; as, the train nosed its way into the statio;
To push or move with the nose or front forward.
q: A train of cable cars came nosing along.

senses.d: One of the external openings of the nose, which give passage to the air breathed and to secretions from the nose and eyes; one of the anterior nares.
Perception; insight; acuteness.
q: Methinks a man Of your sagacity and clear nostril should Have made another choice.

Nostril.etym: [OE. nosethril, nosethirl, AS. nosþyrl; nos for nosu nose + þyrel opening, hole, from þyrel pierced, for þyrhel, fr. purh through. √261. See Nose, and Through, and cf. Thrill.]

senses.d: Wot not; know not; knows not.
Shorn; shaven.
A word used to express negation, prohibition, denial, or refusal.
q: Not one word spake he more than was need.
Thou shalt not steal.
Thine eyes are upon me, and I am not.
The question is, may I do it, or may I not do it?

Not.etym: [OE. not, noht, nought, naught, the same word as E. naught. See Naught.]

senses.d: Capable of being noted; noticeable; plain; evident.
Worthy of notice; remarkable; memorable; noted or distinguished; as, a notable event, person.
Well-known; notorious.

Notable.etym: [F. notable, L. notabilis, fr. notare to mark, nota mark, note. See 5th Note.]

senses.d: A person, or thing, of distinction.
One of a number of persons, before the revolution of 1789, chiefly of the higher orders, appointed by the king to constitute a representative body.
To butt; to push with the horns.

Note.etym: [AS. hnītan to strike against, imp. hnāt.]

senses.d: Know not; knows not.

Note.etym: [AS. nāt; ne not + wāt wot. See Not, and Wot.]

senses.d: Nut.
Need; needful business.
A mark or token by which a thing may be known; a visible sign; a character; a distinctive mark or feature; a characteristic quality.
q: Whosoever appertain to the visible body of the church, they have also the notes of external profession.
She has the note of possession, the note of freedom from party titles,the note of life — a tough life and a vigorous.
What a note of youth, of imagination, of impulsive eagerness, there was through it all !

senses.d: A mark, or sign, made to call attention, to point out something to notice, or the like; a sign, or token, proving or giving evidence.
A brief remark; a marginal comment or explanation; hence, an annotation on a text or author; a comment; a critical, explanatory, or illustrative observation.
q: The best writers have been perplexed with notes, and obscured with illustrations.

senses.d: A brief writing intended to assist the memory; a memorandum; a minute.

Hence, a writing intended to be used in speaking; memoranda to assist a speaker, being either a synopsis, or the full text of what is to be said; as, to preach from notes; also, a reporter's memoranda; the original report of a speech or of proceedings.
A short informal letter; a billet.
A diplomatic missive or written communication.
A written or printed paper acknowledging a debt, and promising payment; as, a promissory note; a note of hand; a negotiable note.
A list of items or of charges; an account.
q: Here is now the smith's note for shoeing.

senses.d: A character, variously formed, to indicate the length of a tone, and variously placed upon the staff to indicate its pitch. Hence:
q: The wakeful bird . . . tunes her nocturnal note.
That note of revolt against the eighteenth century, which we detect in Goethe, was struck by Winckelmann.

senses.d: Observation; notice; heed.
q: Give orders to my servants that they take No note at all of our being absent hence.

senses.d: Notification; information; intelligence.
q: The king . . . shall have note of this.

Note.etym: [F. note, L. nota; akin to noscere, notum, to know. See Know.]

senses.d: To notice with care; to observe; to remark; to heed; to attend to.
q: No more of that; I have noted it well.

senses.d: To record in writing; to make a memorandum of.
q: Every unguarded word . . . was noted down.

senses.d: To charge, as with crime (with of or for before the thing charged); to brand.
q: They were both noted of incontinency.

senses.d: To denote; to designate.
To annotate.
To set down in musical characters.

Note.etym: [F. noter, L. notare, fr. nota. See Note, n.]

senses.d: Well known by reputation or report; eminent; celebrated; as, a noted author, or traveler.
Not anything; no thing (in the widest sense of the word thing); — opposed to anything and something.
q: Yet had his aspect nothing of severe.

senses.d: Nonexistence; nonentity; absence of being; nihility; nothingness.
A thing of no account, value, or note; something irrelevant and impertinent; something of comparative unimportance; utter insignificance; a trifle.
q: Behold, ye are of nothing, and your work of nought.
'T is nothing, says the fool; but, says the friend, This nothing, sir, will bring you to your end.

senses.d: A cipher; naught.
In no degree; not at all; in no wise.
q: Adam, with such counsel nothing swayed.
The influence of reason in producing our passions is nothing near so extensive as is commonly believed.

senses.d: The act of noting, remarking, or observing; observation by the senses or intellect; cognizance; note.
q: How ready is envy to mingle with the notices we take of other persons !

senses.d: Intelligence, by whatever means communicated; knowledge given or received; means of knowledge; express notification; announcement; warning.
q: I . . . have given him notice that the Duke of Cornwall and Regan his duchess will be here.

senses.d: An announcement, often accompanied by comments or remarks; as, book notices; theatrical notices.
A writing communicating information or warning.
Attention; respectful treatment; civility.

Notice.syn: Attention; regard; remark; note; heed; consideration; respect; civility; intelligence; advice; news.
Notice.etym: [F., fr. L. notitia a being known, knowledge, fr. noscere, notum, to know. See Know.]

senses.d: To observe; to see; to mark; to take note of; to heed; to pay attention to.
To show that one has observed; to take public note of; remark upon; to make comments on; to refer to; as, to notice a book.
q: This plant deserves to be noticed in this place.
Another circumstance was noticed in connection with the suggestion last discussed.

senses.d: To treat with attention and civility; as, to notice strangers.

Notice.syn: To remark; observe; perceive; see; mark; note; mind; regard; heed; mention. See Remark.

senses.d: Without prevention, or obstruction from or by; in spite of.
q: We gentil women bee Loth to displease any wight, Notwithstanding our great right.
Those on whom Christ bestowed miraculous cures were so transported that their gratitude made them, notwithstanding his prohibition, proclaim the wonders he had done.

senses.d: Nevertheless; however; although; as, I shall go, notwithstanding it rains.
q: I will surely rend the kingdom from thee, and will give it to thy servant. Notwithstanding, in thy days I will not do it.
They which honor the law as an image of the wisdom of God himself, are, notwithstanding, to know that the same had an end in Christ.
You did wisely and honestly too, notwithstanding She is the greatest beauty in the parish.
These days were ages to him, notwithstanding that he was basking in the smiles of the pretty Mary.

Notwithstanding.etym: [Originally the participle of withstand, with not prefixed.]

senses.d: To feed and cause to grow; to supply with matter which increases bulk or supplies waste, and promotes health; to furnish with nutriment.
q: He planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it.

senses.d: To support; to maintain.
q: Whiles I in Ireland nourish a mighty band.

senses.d: To supply the means of support and increase to; to encourage; to foster; as, to nourish rebellion; to nourish the virtues.
To cherish; to comfort.
q: Ye have nourished your hearts.

senses.d: To educate; to instruct; to bring up; to nurture; to promote the growth of in attainments.
q: Nourished up in the words of faith.

Nourish.syn: To cherish; feed; supply. See Nurture.
Nourish.etym: [OE. norisen, norischen, OF. nurir, nurrir, norir, F. nourrir, fr. L. nutrire. Cf. Nurse, Nutriment, and see -ish.]

senses.d: To promote growth; to furnish nutriment.
q: Grains and roots nourish more than their leaves.

senses.d: To gain nourishment.
A nurse.
One who, or that which, nourishes.
Promoting growth; nutritious.
The act of nourishing, or the state of being nourished; nutrition.
That which serves to nourish; nutriment; food.
q: Learn to seek the nourishment of their souls.

senses.d: One who is new in any business, profession, or calling; one unacquainted or unskilled; one yet in the rudiments; a beginner; a tyro.
q: I am young; a novice in the trade.

senses.d: One newly received into the church, or one newly converted to the Christian faith.
One who enters a religious house, whether of monks or nuns, as a probationist.
q: No poore cloisterer, nor no novys.

Novice.etym: [F., from L. novicius, novitius, new, from novus new. See New, and cf. Novitious.]

senses.d: Like a novice; becoming a novice.
At the present time; at this moment; at the time of speaking; instantly; as, I will write now.
q: I have a patient now living, at an advanced age, who discharged blood from his lungs thirty years ago.

senses.d: Very lately; not long ago.
q: They that but now, for honor and for plate, Made the sea blush with blood, resign their hate.

senses.d: At a time contemporaneous with something spoken of or contemplated; at a particular time referred to.
q: The ship was now in the midst of the sea.

senses.d: In present circumstances; things being as they are; — hence, used as a connective particle, to introduce an inference or an explanation.
q: How shall any man distinguish now betwixt a parasite and a man of honor ?
Why should he live, now nature bankrupt is ?
Then cried they all again, saying, Not this man, but Barabbas. Now, Barabbas was a robber.
The other great and undoing mischief which befalls men is, by their being misrepresented. Now, by calling evil good, a man is misrepresented to others in the way of slander.

Now.etym: [OE. nou, nu, AS. nū, nu; akin to D., OS., & OHG. nu, G. nu, nun, Icel., nū, Dan., Sw., & Goth. nu, L. nunc, Gr. νύ, νυ̑ν, Skr. nu, nū. √193. Cf. New.]

senses.d: Existing at the present time; present.
The present time or moment; the present.
q: Nothing is there to come, and nothing past; But an eternal now does ever last.

senses.d: Enfeebled in, or destitute of, the power of sensation and motion; rendered torpid; benumbed; insensible; as, the fingers or limbs are numb with cold.
Producing numbness; benumbing; as, the numb, cold night.

Numb.etym: [OE. nume, nome, prop., seized, taken, p. p. of nimen to take, AS. niman, p. p. numen. √7. See Nimble, Nomad, and cf. Benumb.]

senses.d: To make numb; to deprive of the power of sensation or motion; to render senseless or inert; to deaden; to benumb; to stupefy.
q: For lazy winter numbs the laboring hand.
Like dull narcotics, numbing pain.

senses.d: That which admits of being counted or reckoned; a unit, or an aggregate of units; a numerable aggregate or collection of individuals; an assemblage made up of distinct things expressible by figures.
A collection of many individuals; a numerous assemblage; a multitude; many.
q: Ladies are always of great use to the party they espouse, and never fail to win over numbers.

senses.d: A numeral; a word or character denoting a number; as, to put a number on a door.
Numerousness; multitude.
q: Number itself importeth not much in armies where the people are of weak courage.

senses.d: The state or quality of being numerable or countable.
q: Of whom came nations, tribes, people, and kindreds out of number.

senses.d: Quantity, regarded as made up of an aggregate of separate things.
That which is regulated by count; poetic measure, as divisions of time or number of syllables; hence, poetry, verse; — chiefly used in the plural.
q: I lisped in numbers, for the numbers came.

senses.d: The distinction of objects, as one, or more than one (in some languages, as one, or two, or more than two), expressed (usually) by a difference in the form of a word; thus, the singular number and the plural number are the names of the forms of a word indicating the objects denoted or referred to by the word as one, or as more than one.
The measure of the relation between quantities or things of the same kind; that abstract species of quantity which is capable of being expressed by figures; numerical value.

Number.etym: [OE. nombre, F. nombre, L. numerus; akin to Gr. νόμοσ that which is dealt out, fr. νέμειν to deal out, distribute. See Numb, Nomad, and cf. Numerate, Numero, Numerous.]

senses.d: To count; to reckon; to ascertain the units of; to enumerate.
q: If a man can number the dust of the earth, then shall thy seed also be numbered.

senses.d: To reckon as one of a collection or multitude.
q: He was numbered with the transgressors.

senses.d: To give or apply a number or numbers to; to assign the place of in a series by order of number; to designate the place of by a number or numeral; as, to number the houses in a street, or the apartments in a building.
To amount; to equal in number; to contain; to consist of; as, the army numbers fifty thousand.
q: Thy tears can not number the dead.

Number.etym: [OE. nombren, noumbren, F. nombrer, fr. L. numerare, numeratum. See Number, n.]

senses.d: A woman devoted to a religious life, who lives in a convent, under the three vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience.
q: They holy time is quiet as a nun Breathless with adoration.

senses.d: A white variety of domestic pigeons having a veil of feathers covering the head.

Nun.etym: [OE. nunne, AS. nunne, fr. L. nonna nun, nonnus monk; cf. Gr. �, �; of unknown origin. Cf. Nunnery.]

senses.d: One who nourishes; a person who supplies food, tends, or brings up; as: (a) A woman who has the care of young children; especially, one who suckles an infant not her own. (b) A person, especially a woman, who has the care of the sick or infirm.
One who, or that which, brings up, rears, causes to grow, trains, fosters, or the like.
q: The nurse of manly sentiment and heroic enterprise.

senses.d: A lieutenant or first officer, who is the real commander when the captain is unfit for his place.
A peculiar larva of certain trematodes which produces cercariæ by asexual reproduction. See Cercaria, and Redia.

Nurse.etym: [OE. nourse, nurice, norice, OF. nurrice, norrice, nourrice, F. nourrice, fr. L. nutricia nurse, prop., fem. of nutricius that nourishes; akin to nutrix, -icis, nurse, fr. nutrire to nourish. See Nourish, and cf. Nutritious.]

senses.d: To nourish; to cherish; to foster
q: Sons wont to nurse their parents in old age.
Him in Egerian groves Aricia bore, And nursed his youth along the marshy shore.

senses.d: To bring up; to raise, by care, from a weak or invalid condition; to foster; to cherish; — applied to plants, animals, and to any object that needs, or thrives by, attention.
q: By what hands been nursed into so uncontrolled a dominion?

senses.d: To manage with care and economy, with a view to increase; as, to nurse our national resources.
To caress; to fondle, as a nurse does.
Supplying or taking nourishment from, or as from, the breast; as, a nursing mother; a nursing infant.
The act of nourishing or nursing; tender care; education; training.
q: A man neither by nature nor by nurture wise.

senses.d: That which nourishes; food; diet.

Nurture.etym: [OE. norture, noriture, OF. norriture, norreture, F. nourriture, fr. L. nutritura a nursing, suckling. See Nourish.]

senses.d: To feed; to nourish.
To educate; to bring or train up.
q: He was nurtured where he had been born.

Nurture.syn: To nourish; nurse; cherish; bring up; educate; tend.

senses.d: The fruit of certain trees and shrubs (as of the almond, walnut, hickory, beech, filbert, etc.), consisting of a hard and indehiscent shell inclosing a kernel.

A perforated block (usually a small piece of metal), provided with an internal or female screw thread, used on a bolt, or screw, for tightening or holding something, or for transmitting motion. See Illust. of 1st Bolt.
The tumbler of a gunlock.
A projection on each side of the shank of an anchor, to secure the stock in place.

Nut.etym: [OE. nute, note, AS. hnutu; akin to D. noot, G. nuss, OHG. nuz, Icel. hnot, Sw. nöt, Dan. nöd.]

senses.d: To gather nuts.
Same as Nymph, 3.
Two folds of mucous membrane, within the labia, at the opening of the vulva.
